After this lecture, you should be able to:

represent vectors in a chosen basis and distinguish a vector from its
components;
test finite sets of vectors for linear independence;
compute norms, dot products, projections, and cross products;
use the conjugated inner product for complex vectors; and
interpret cross and scalar-triple products geometrically.
A vector is a quantity that requires both a magnitude

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d.art3d import Poly3DCollection

GOLD = "#cfb991"
DARK_GOLD = "#8e6f3e"
BLACK = "#000000"
GRAY = "#6f727b"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 120,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.22,
})

The parallelogram and head-to-tail constructions are shown together, making it
clear that addition combines displacements rather than merely adding columns.

a = np.array([3.0, 1.0])
b = np.array([1.0, 2.4])
s = a + b

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.2))
ax.quiver(0, 0, *a, angles="xy", scale_units="xy", scale=1,
          color=BLACK, width=0.012, label=r"$\mathbf{a}$")
ax.quiver(0, 0, *b, angles="xy", scale_units="xy", scale=1,
          color=GOLD, width=0.012, label=r"$\mathbf{b}$")
ax.quiver(*a, *b, angles="xy", scale_units="xy", scale=1,
          color=GOLD, width=0.010, alpha=0.75)
ax.quiver(*b, *a, angles="xy", scale_units="xy", scale=1,
          color=BLACK, width=0.010, alpha=0.55)
ax.quiver(0, 0, *s, angles="xy", scale_units="xy", scale=1,
          color=DARK_GOLD, width=0.014, label=r"$\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$")
ax.plot([a[0], s[0], b[0]], [a[1], s[1], b[1]], "--", color=GRAY)
ax.set(aspect="equal", xlim=(-0.4, 4.8), ylim=(-0.4, 4.2),
       xlabel="$x$", ylabel="$y$", title="Vector addition: two equivalent paths")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

This diagram separates a vector into the part parallel to another vector and a
perpendicular residual. It directly supports dot products and least squares.

v = np.array([3.6, 3.0])
u = np.array([4.2, 1.2])
projection = (v @ u) / (u @ u) * u
residual = v - projection

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.7, 5.0))
line_t = np.linspace(-0.15, 1.35, 100)
ax.plot(line_t*u[0], line_t*u[1], color=GRAY, linewidth=2, label="span of u")
for start, vec, color, label in [
    (np.zeros(2), v, BLACK, r"$\mathbf{v}$"),
    (np.zeros(2), projection, DARK_GOLD, r"$\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v}$"),
    (projection, residual, GOLD, "orthogonal residual"),
]:
    ax.quiver(*start, *vec, angles="xy", scale_units="xy", scale=1,
              color=color, width=0.012, label=label)
ax.scatter(*projection, color=DARK_GOLD, s=55, zorder=3)
ax.set(aspect="equal", xlim=(-0.4, 5.2), ylim=(-0.4, 4.1),
       xlabel="$x$", ylabel="$y$", title="A vector decomposed into parallel and perpendicular parts")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
plt.show()

The two input vectors span a parallelogram, while their cross product points
normal to it. Reversing the order reverses the normal but not the area.

a3 = np.array([2.4, 0.4, 0.2])
b3 = np.array([0.5, 1.8, 0.7])
cross = np.cross(a3, b3)
corners = np.array([[0,0,0], a3, a3+b3, b3])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.2, 5.7))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
ax.add_collection3d(Poly3DCollection([corners], facecolor=GOLD,
                                     edgecolor=DARK_GOLD, alpha=0.35))
for vec, color, label in [(a3, BLACK, "a"), (b3, GRAY, "b"),
                          (cross, DARK_GOLD, "a × b")]:
    ax.quiver(0, 0, 0, *vec, color=color, linewidth=2,
              arrow_length_ratio=0.12, label=label)
ax.set(xlim=(0, 3.3), ylim=(0, 2.6), zlim=(0, 4.3),
       xlabel="$x$", ylabel="$y$", zlabel="$z$",
       title=rf"$|\mathbf{{a}}\times\mathbf{{b}}|={np.linalg.norm(cross):.2f}$ is the parallelogram area")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

Two panels contrast a genuine three-dimensional basis with three coplanar
vectors. The scalar triple product provides an immediate numerical diagnostic.

sets = [
    (np.array([[1,0,0], [0.3,1,0], [0.2,0.2,1.1]]), "independent"),
    (np.array([[1,0,0], [0.3,1,0], [0.65,0.5,0]]), "dependent"),
]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4.8))
for index, (vectors, label) in enumerate(sets, start=1):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, index, projection="3d")
    for vector, color in zip(vectors, [BLACK, DARK_GOLD, GOLD]):
        ax.quiver(0, 0, 0, *vector, color=color, linewidth=2,
                  arrow_length_ratio=0.12)
    volume = abs(np.linalg.det(vectors))
    ax.set(xlim=(0,1.3), ylim=(0,1.3), zlim=(0,1.3),
           xlabel="$x$", ylabel="$y$", zlabel="$z$",
           title=f"{label}: |det| = {volume:.2f}")
fig.suptitle("Linear independence creates volume")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
